title: Mary Peltola unseats Sen. Dan Sullivan, giving Dems a 56-seat Senate majority
summary: It's the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state.
content: Former Rep. Mary Peltola ousted GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska — the first time in 18 years a Democrat has won a Senate race in the state. Her win gives Democrats a 56-44 edge in the Senate. Peltola was one of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s top recruits for the cycle. She overpowered a Republican rescue mission for Sullivan and allegations of misconduct against her from former staffers to flip a state President Donald Trump won by 13 points in 2024. Her victory continues the blue wave born from voters’ frustrations at high costs and the Trump administration. Peltola will return to Washington, where she will become the first Alaska Native to serve in the Senate after previously holding the same distinction in the House. Her campaign had projected confidence about her path to victory as the vote count dragged on in a far-flung, rural state with long grace periods for late-arriving ballots. But her win was not without tumult. Trump’s Department of Justice sued to try to stop the certification if Sullivan lost, claiming voters could be confused by his same-name challenger. The president went so far as to call for votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan and another longshot candidate in the four-way, all-party contest to be transferred to the incumbent. The Justice Department also started probing efforts to recruit Dan J. Sullivan after a New York Times report suggesting members of Peltola’s campaign and Senate Democrats’ campaign arm were involved. Both had previously denied involvement.

title: Bo French loses Texas country club membership
summary: The anti-immigrant Texas Republican had his membership at a historic Fort Worth country club terminated days after a bruising electoral defeat.
content: Bo French, the far-right firebrand who centered his losing campaign for the Texas Railroad Commission on his anti-immigration stance, lost his membership at a Fort Worth country club, according to a letter obtained by POLITICO . The letter from River Crest Country Club, dated Nov. 10 and addressed to French, said the club’s board of directors voted to terminate French’s membership immediately “for reasons relating to the reputation and general welfare of the Club.” French said Wednesday on social media that the board asked him to resign in September due to "racist posts." He said he refused to do so, leading to an expulsion meeting. "Nothing I said in September was racist," he said in a published statement that he read to the board. The country club, founded in 1911, is the eighth to open in the state and boasts being a “who’s who” of Fort Worth. It hosts a 6,368-yard golf course that has been a training ground for top golfers, according to its website. River Crest declined to comment, citing its policy of not doing so about “past, present and prospective members” and club operations, its general manager said in an email. French, who has a history of making controversial statements on immigration issues like the H-1B visa program, made headlines in September after going viral on social media for a post he made that appeared to disparage Asian American students at the University of Texas at Austin. His remarks capitalized on the growing anti-Indian sentiment sweeping Texas and across the nation , particularly against holders of the high-skilled worker visa, a majority of whom are from India. The post quickly drew rebukes from Democrats and some Texas Republicans, who denounced it as racist. But French stood by the post . He said he was criticizing admission and hiring policies at UT, the state’s public flagship, that he claimed discriminated against Texas residents. (State law requires a majority of admitted students at the school to be residents of the state.) French lost by 677,000 votes in his bid to sit on the influential statewide body that regulates Texas’ oil and gas industry two months later amid a statewide wipeout for the GOP. He previously led the Tarrant County Republican Party and also had two unsuccessful state House bids. French did not respond to requests for comment sent to multiple email addresses associated with him. Ashley Ahn contributed reporting.
authors: By Casey He and Jonathan Martin

title: This new early-state governor has advice for 2028 Democratic hopefuls
summary: New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland told POLITICO she would 'love' to endorse in her state’s newly-minted early primary.
content: Deb Haaland is about to take the helm of a newly-minted Democratic presidential primary battleground. She has thoughts for her party’s White House hopefuls on how to win there. Haaland, New Mexico’s incoming governor, told POLITICO that immigration will be a “top issue” in the presidential election — one that she’s “anxious” to see how future candidates plan to address — and said that engaging with rural voters in her state will be key to any successful primary campaign. “New Mexico is the fifth largest state, and we are largely rural,” Haaland told POLITICO’s Erin Doherty in an onstage interview at the National Governors Association's New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. “There are far more rural communities than there are large cities in our state, and so this will be important for New Mexicans to to really understand or to really know that any presidential candidate understands the challenges that they're facing.” Immigration is “going to be a top issue with the 2028 presidential election,” she added. “New Mexico is an early primary state, and it happens that we're a border state, too.” Haaland’s ascension to the governor’s mansion coincides with a major change in New Mexico’s place in the Democratic Party's presidential nominating calendar pecking order. The state will now be fourth in the voting calendar behind South Carolina, Nevada and New Hampshire. The move gives New Mexicans — and their new governor — significant influence in shaping the kind of nominee the party selects to take back the White House. It’ll also pose a significant test for candidate’s engagement with Latino voters, as New Mexico ranks first nationwide in its population share of Latino residents. Some of those potential candidates have already come calling. “Rahm Emanuel was in New Mexico, and he did quite a bit of traveling around,” Haaland said, noting that several senators made their own sojourns to the state for an event hosted in October by Democratic Sen. Ben Ray Luján in Alberquerque. Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg made his own trip to the state in September. “Whether all of them are running for president, I can't tell you, but I am really anxious to see who does.” Haaland, a former Secretary of the Interior and the first Native American woman elected to a governorship, is ready to wield her own influence in the process as well, flexing her new power broker status . “I would love to endorse, but I'll wait and see who throws their hat in the ring,” she said. Haaland was swept into office with a historic number of fellow Democrats across the country on a mandate to deliver on affordability. It’s the “biggest issue” in New Mexico, Haaland said, adding that her priority to deliver lower costs for New Mexicans will start with expanding access to affordable health care. “Right now we're talking with some of the leaders in the legislature about health care, a public option for people in New Mexico,” she said. “Health care is a top top priority.”

title: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
summary: Republicans and Democrats are split over the future direction of their parties, but Americans broadly agree the GOP’s prospects are in doubt, a new POLITICO Poll shows.
content: Nearly twice as many Americans expect a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028 than they do a Republican, a new POLITICO Poll finds . Even one in five of President Donald Trump’s own 2024 voters believe Republicans will lose the White House, a bad sign for the GOP as it struggles to recover from widespread losses this cycle and figure out its identity after spending a decade orbiting around Trump. Just 60% of Trump voters believe Republicans will keep the White House. Democratic voters are far more confident about their own party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global in the days after the midterm: Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, 87% expect Democrats to win in 2028. Beneath the unity is disagreement over what kind of nominee to pick. Pluralities of voters agree the next president should be a fighter when asked to choose from a list of qualities. But voters across the ideological spectrum also said they want other things from the country’s 48th president. While 43% of Harris voters want “a fighter,” 40% also selected “a progressive” and 34% chose “creative.” Among Trump voters, the 45% said they want to see “a conservative” elected president, surpassing the 39% who picked “a fighter.” They're also divided over what background their nominees should come from. Nearly three in 10 Trump voters say they would prefer the next president be someone who has not worked in Trump’s administration. That number rises to 46% among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA, whereas 82% of his loyal MAGA base would prefer the next president be someone who did work for Trump. That debate is playing out in real-time among top GOP leaders and lawmakers. More and more Hill Republicans are eyeing Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 2028, who they say is less associated with the midterm bloodbath than Vice President JD Vance. Others say the nominee should be someone entirely outside of Trump’s direct orbit. “As much as I like Rubio, and as much as I like Vance, they can't be our nominee,” said Dan McMaster, the chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party. “We need to get a Republican as far away from Trump as possible, and even then, I think it's going to be a battle.” “You've got to have some fresh blood in there, and you've got to have someone that has some distance from the crap that's gone on the last two years,” said one GOP strategist who worked on multiple House races last cycle and was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party. In a statement, Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said the president isn’t going anywhere. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs, and secured our border,” Baldassarre said. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028." The White House also pointed POLITICO to separate polling earlier this month that shows Trump’s approval rating sits at 75% with all Republicans and jumps to 93% with those who identify as MAGA. “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. On election night earlier this month, Trump blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot, telling POLITICO by phone , “I wasn't on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, we would have won; we would have won it all very easily.” Meanwhile, Democrats have their own disagreements to figure out as they select their nominee. This cycle’s blue wave has bolstered the progressive wing of the party, which has long hoped to prove their candidates can win in purple battlegrounds, not just in safe-blue states. But the poll reveals skepticism remains — at least among moderates — over whether progressive wins in 2026 can translate to the presidential stage in 2028. The survey found a majority of progressive Democrats — 63% — want a progressive to be president, compared with just 23% of moderates who say the same. Half of progressive Democrats are convinced that being a progressive is a quality that will get their candidate elected in 2028. Moderates are less certain of that, though they’re also not as confident in their own faction: Just 37% think being a moderate is a quality that ensures the Democratic candidate wins. “Whoever's running for president has seen what's happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” said progressive New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, reflecting on the wins he and others enjoyed this cycle. “Despite it being the most expensive elections in history, we showed that people are able to beat out money when we come together.” And with Democrats winning Senate seats in deep-red states like Kansas and Mississippi for the first time in decades, many now argue that the entire map is in play for 2028. The poll found that 60% of Democrats think the party should focus their efforts on winning all states in the presidential election, even ones that seemed like deep Republican areas, rather than focus on holding the states where they know their supporters are. Republicans felt the same, with 56% also arguing for an “all states” approach as the party races to rebuild in territory they once thought was safe. “I have been very, very loud about the fact that the path to the presidency leads through the South,” said Democratic strategist Dallas Jones, who ran statewide Black voter engagement for Lone Star Rising PAC, the outside group that supported Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. “But again, we don't make investments there. We're playing the same electoral map with the same swing states.”

title: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno, the incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, is clear-eyed on the challenges ahead as the party reckons with midterm losses.
content: Sen. Bernie Moreno isn’t sugarcoating things. The incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee will be in charge of defending 19 GOP seats in 2028 — and he’ll need to flip at least six more to regain control of the Senate majority. “Looking at it right now, it's absolutely a savagely brutal map,” the Ohio Republican said in an interview on Capitol Hill. After a historic midterms shellacking, Moreno is in the hot seat as he looks to navigate his chamber — and the party — through a rebuilding of its brand and its base over next two years. Republicans will likely have just 44 seats heading into 2028. They need to hold onto seats in battleground states like Wisconsin and North Carolina, while trying to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly in Arizona, John Fetterman in Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock in Georgia and Catherine Cortez Masto in Nevada. Moreno and his team have interviewed a handful of candidates over the last few days to be the next NRSC executive director, according to four people with direct knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. Republicans expect Chris Grant, a former Moreno and Trump campaign staffer who now runs his own firm, to serve as a main outside GOP consultant for the committee. On top of the grueling map ahead, the Ohio Republican is facing the additional task of working with a lame duck president who still wields immense power over the GOP and its primaries. Then there’s the vice president, who is likely to run for president himself in the same two-year sprint. Moreno is close with both of those men. Asked how involved he expects the White House to be in GOP primaries and recruiting going forward, he replied, “We’re going to work on all of that.” It’ll be a complicated path forward. Moreno, over the past cycle has been unwilling to cast blame on President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance. Days before the midterm elections, he said if Republicans lost, it would be because people were “pissed off” about high gas prices. He’s unlikely to completely distance himself and the NRSC brand from the president's influence. But the party is currently undergoing a reckoning of how closely to align with the president after voters delivered an uncompromising rebuke of Trump’s economic agenda. Across the country, several battlegrounds and once-thought-to-be-safe red territory fell to Democratic hands. Trump in the 2026 cycle angered many Senate Republicans by supporting a primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn of Texas — a move they privately say cost them north of $200 million as they tried, in vain, to save Ken Paxton’s imperiled campaign. The president also supported a primary challenge against Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, and pushed Sen. Thom Tillis to decide to retire in highly competitive North Carolina. One of the biggest challenges before Moreno and Senate Republicans after the midterms wipeout is to find candidates who can win a general election in highly competitive states, while also making it through GOP primaries where Trump will be a major factor. They’ll need to push back on the White House if the president tries, once again, to intervene — though that’s easier said than done. “There will be no patience for bad recruits this cycle,” said one senior Republican granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations, referring to the implosions of Paxton, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and other Republicans who were hand-picked by Trump. The White House referred POLITICO to Trump's post-midterms comments, where he blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot and said he brought several candidates "closer to victory," though they ultimately lost. Senate Majority Leader John Thune — who will be the minority leader next year — and his team plan to be heavily involved in recruitment efforts, according to two people involved in the conversations, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Their goal, one of the people said, is “to make sure we have our strongest possible candidates on the ballot in 2028.” Moreno is already trying to find a GOP recruit in his home state of Ohio to run against incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, whose term will be up again in 2028 after he won a special election against GOP Sen. Jon Husted earlier this month. The new NRSC chair said he’s looking for “somebody who can beat the crap out of Sherrod Brown.” Husted in private conversations hasn’t completely ruled out another bid, but he’s indicated he’s unlikely to run again, according to three people with knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Ohio Republicans expect former state Sen. Kevin Coughlin to explore a potential Senate bid. And they’re watching Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), who just lost his reelection. Husted did not respond to a request for comment. A Turner spokesperson said in a statement that the representative "has been approached by several people about this and is keeping all his options open.” If Vance doesn’t seek his own presidential bid, Republicans in his home state are holding a long-shot hope that he, too, might consider a return to his old job. “JD Vance would be a dream candidate,” said one Ohio Republican. A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score . Want to receive the newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro . You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.

title: Utah GOP governor on Trump and 2028: ‘It’s time for the next thing’
summary: Gov. Spencer Cox said he’s 'a fan of governors' as he eyes the party’s options for a 2028 nominee.
content: Utah’s Republican governor wants his party to move beyond President Donald Trump heading into the next presidential election. “It’s time for the next thing,” Gov. Spencer Cox said in an interview on Wednesday at the POLITICO Pub, on the sidelines of the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in Deer Valley, Utah. Cox called on his fellow Republicans to start looking for new leadership in the wake of this month’s midterm election defeats. “This is how this works when presidents move on. We should be looking for the next leadership in our party and what that looks like,” Cox told POLITICO’s Samuel Benson. “We’ve got JD Vance and Marco Rubio, and those seem to be kind of the two choices now,” Cox said, referring to the Vice President and Secretary of State, respectively. “But I think you’ll see a lot of people step up … there are a lot of really interesting folks.” “I’m a fan of governors,” Cox added. “I think governors with executive experience are the best to lead the country.” Vance told Fox News earlier this week that he would decide “sometime next year” whether he will run for president in 2028. Rubio has dismissed suggestions that he would launch his own bid, and has said he would support Vance if the Vice President ran for the White House. “I am hopeful that there are some Republican governors that will throw their hat in,” said Cox, a two-term governor. “We can have a competition of ideas heading in to find out what's next.” Cox said that Trump still has a “really important role to play” in leading the party over the next two years, adding that the president still had an “opportunity” to strike bipartisan deals on permitting reform and other policy areas in his last two years in office. Cox called the president “unique,” adding: “He’s someone who has the attention of the country in a way that almost no president has had in my lifetime.” “People really love him or really don’t like him, but everybody’s paying attention to him,” he said.
